2.0.s.en: (1) God's rebuke for their not driving out the pagans

2.0.0.en: An angel: either God appeared in the form of an angel, or a real angel speaking a message from God.

2.0.1.en: Bochim: it lies near Bethel and is higher than the land surrounding it, and the meaning of its name is the weepers, because the people of God wept there (v. 5). I will never break: I will not go back on My covenant.

2.0.2.en: God had appeared in the form of an angel at Gilgal to Joshua (Josh 5:13; 6:2), and now He goes up from Gilgal to appear to the people at a place called Bochim, and reminds them that He had brought them up out of the land of Egypt, where Pharaoh had enslaved them, and had fulfilled His promise to their fathers by giving them the land of Canaan. He had promised them that He would never break His covenant with them, and of course this is on condition that they obey His commandments. God fulfilled this with the new Israel, that is, the Christians, transferring them to Paradise and giving them the Kingdom of Heaven, that they may reign with Him forever.

2.1.0.en: God commanded them not to make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land from among the pagan peoples and not to mingle with them, but to throw down their altars so that every trace of paganism would vanish. But despite the Lord's repeated warnings they did not heed His counsel; rather they allowed them to dwell in their midst and mingled with them, as we saw in the previous chapter. The question here is one of rebuke, showing the Lord's astonishment and displeasure at their deeds.

2.2.0.en: A snare: a trap and a stumbling block.

2.2.1.en: The Lord's response to their disobedience was only to let them reap the reward of this disobedience, so that the recompense would be of the same kind as their deed: those peoples whom they left in their midst would become a source of disturbance and trouble to them in the future, fighting them and plundering their possessions. Indeed, the gods those peoples worship would be a snare and a stumbling block to the children of Israel, as those peoples would draw them to become like them and to share in their worship, forsaking the worship of the true God.

2.3.0.en: When they heard this message from the Lord, they were deeply moved and repented of their deeds and of their disobedience to His guidance. In remembrance of their grief and weeping they called the name of the place "Bochim", a Hebrew word meaning weepers. And they offered sacrifices there to atone for their sin.

2.3.1.en: The sacrifices used to be offered on the altar of God in Shiloh, but because God appeared in this place, they made a temporary altar and offered the sacrifices on it, and this was an exception.

2.3.2.en: It should be noted that despite the weeping and the remorse, the people did not move to drive out the pagans from among them according to the Lord's message to them. For to be content with weeping, without hope and without the work of repentance, changes nothing in God's sight; it is a false repentance.

2.3.3.en: May your repentance be joined with works that confirm it, so that you put right your wrongs, that is, you apologize to the one you wronged or return what you stole... in addition to drawing near to God through holy acts of worship in which your love for Him appears, so that your repentance is a true repentance.

2.4.0.en: A generation that did not know the Lord: it seems that the fathers failed to teach their children faith in God and His works with His people, so that when the generation that was contemporary with Joshua died, and the elders who were contemporary with him, the devout ones who had taught the people, this new generation neglected the teaching of its children, and they drifted away from the knowledge of God and the keeping of His commandments. Timnath-heres: it means the portion of the sun, and it was mentioned in (Josh 34:3) as Timnath-serah, meaning a double portion; perhaps they changed the name of the city to the portion of the sun after Joshua stopped the sun in his war with the five kings (Map 12). This is a repetition of what is in (Josh 24:28-31...); refer to the Book of Joshua.

2.4.1.en: The repetition by the inspired writer here is for a spiritual wisdom, which is to remind the people of their spiritual state in the days of Joshua and the glory they achieved in their wars against the pagan peoples, so that they might compare what was then with what is happening now, in that they have allowed the pagan peoples to remain in the land in their midst, contrary to the divine command.

2.5.s.en: (2) The pagans' attacks on the people of God

2.5.0.en: Baalim: the plural of Baal, a famous pagan god.

2.5.1.en: From this verse to the end of the chapter, the picture of the life the people lived in the period called the era of the Judges is brought together. This verse tells us that the children of Israel committed the great sin which the Lord had forbidden repeatedly, and which was the first commandment of the Ten Commandments, which calls for the worship of the true God alone, without the false pagan gods. So the people betrayed God and worshiped those false gods.

2.6.0.en: They forsook the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who loved them and freed them from slavery in the land of Egypt, for He brought them out from there with signs and wonders and brought them to a land flowing with milk and honey to possess it. They imitated the other peoples whom they had left in their midst in worshiping false gods and bowed down to them, forgetting the first commandment the Lord had given them at Sinai, and by this they disobeyed God and defied Him.

2.7.0.en: Ashtaroth: she is the chief goddess in Babylon and Assyria, the mother of the goddesses, and her worship involves very licentious practices, and her priestesses were harlots, because she is always worshiped together with a male god, Baal, the husband of Ashtaroth and lord of fertility, and human sacrifices were offered to him.

2.7.1.en: Gathered unto his fathers: he died and was buried with his fathers.

2.7.2.en: They abandoned the worship of the living God and worshiped false gods that the pagan peoples worshiped, such as Baal and Ashtaroth.

2.8.0.en: The Lord was greatly angered against them, so He left their enemies to plunder their wealth and the produce of their land and to take their wives and children as male and female slaves. God did not defend them as He used to before; rather divine providence forsook them, so they became unable to repel their enemies and protect themselves.

2.9.0.en: He delivered them into the hands of spoilers: He handed them over to the might of their enemies who plundered them.

2.9.1.en: The hand of the Lord was against them for evil: the hand of the Lord is a figure for the power and work of the Lord, so the Lord was working against them for harm and to bring evil and woe upon them.

2.9.2.en: Wherever they went, whether to carry on their daily work, or to trade with the surrounding peoples, or to face their enemies and fight them, in every case the Lord allowed them to be hurt by everything harmful and injurious. In this the Lord did not take them by surprise, for He had warned them again and again against breaking their covenant with Him, and had cautioned them that He would punish them most severely if they broke the covenant, so they were greatly distressed by the pagans' humiliation of them.

2.9.3.en: Do not persist in your sins and your disobedience to God, defying Him and provoking Him, for who are you that you should resist God? But if you sin because of your weakness, repent quickly, for His mercies are many, and He cares for His weak children and forgives them all their sins.

2.10.s.en: (3) The raising up of judges to deliver them

2.10.0.en: When the people of God were distressed they cried out to Him, so He raised up judges for them from among them, who judged by His law, led their armies and delivered them from their enemies.

2.11.0.en: After God freed them by means of the judge and they kept His commandments, they would turn back and forsake God's teachings which they had heard from the mouth of the judge, and worship idols, resembling a woman who commits adultery and leaves her husband, and by this they had forsaken the way of their devout fathers who worshiped God.

2.12.0.en: The Lord repented because of their groaning: this is a figurative expression in our human language, for the Lord is not moved by passions as human beings are. The intended meaning is that the Lord hears His people when they cry out to Him repenting of their deeds, and He prepares for them someone to rescue them.

2.13.0.en: After the death of the judge they would turn away from the Lord and return to their sins, and even go further in them than those before them had done. They worshiped the pagan gods and did not cease from their evil deeds and the hardness of their hearts.

2.13.1.en: Do not waver between good and evil, worshiping God while at the same time allowing yourself some sins, or offering repentance and then returning to sin through negligence. Ask God's help that you may remain firm in the life with Him and enjoy His fellowship.

2.14.s.en: (4) The pagans left with the people of God

2.14.0.en: Because the people of God allowed themselves the worship of idols, did not remain firm in repentance and broke their covenant with Him, God decided, as a punishment for them, to leave the pagans dwelling among them and troubling them, that perhaps they might repent with a true repentance.

2.15.0.en: God's purpose in not helping them to drive out the pagans was to test His people, whether they would worship Him faithfully and keep His commandments, so that He would help them to drive out the enemies, or would be negligent in worshiping Him, so that He would allow the enemies to humiliate them.

2.16.0.en: God left the pagan peoples in the days of Joshua, since his old age did not allow him to complete the driving out of all the pagans, and this was a test for the people, whether they would obey God's word through the mouth of Joshua and complete the liberation of their land, or be negligent. Sadly they were negligent, so the enemies troubled them greatly in the era of the Judges, but for the sake of David's righteousness, God helped him to drive out these peoples.

2.16.1.en: Our repeated transgressions of God's commandments provoke divine anger against us, and then we return and complain, asking why the Lord is angry... Earnestness in repentance is what draws God's help, and by it victory is achieved.

2.16.2.en: The judges Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar. From this chapter to (ch. 16) the judges are recounted: when their people grew negligent, the pagan peoples rose against them and humiliated them, so they cried out to God and He sent them the judge who delivered them, but they returned and grew negligent, so the pagan peoples humiliated them, and so on.

3.0.s.en: (1) The peoples who remained in the midst of Israel

3.0.0.en: The people of God were negligent in completing the driving out of the wicked inhabitants of the land, so they dwelt beside them. These peoples had not known the wars that took place at the hand of Joshua, either because they did not believe them or because they had not witnessed them, so they made light of them and did not fear God, who leads His people and protects them. God allowed them to remain in order to test His people, that is, to make them know the consequences of their negligence in carrying out His commandments. For these peoples enticed them to worship their idols and they intermarried with them, so God forsook them and these peoples humiliated them.

3.1.0.en: Only: the men who had not taken part in the previous wars.

3.1.1.en: Here he makes clear a principal reason for God's allowing these peoples to remain with His people: that the men of His people who had not taken part in the previous wars, because of their youth, might learn how to fight these peoples and drive them out, so as to possess their land and fulfill God's promise, through their reliance on God, their seeking help from His power in war, and their upright conduct. By this they would always be ready and not become slack. This shows how God turns their sin, which was the negligence in leaving the pagans, into a blessing by teaching them vigilance and constant readiness.

3.2.1.en: The five: this means the rulers of the five famous Philistine cities, which are Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron. They lie between the Brook of Egypt in the north of Egypt and Ekron in the north (Josh 13:3). The Canaanites: they represent the original inhabitants of the Promised Land, who were spread throughout its regions.

3.2.2.en: The Hivites: one of the Canaanite tribes, who lived in the villages that are in Mount Lebanon.

3.2.3.en: The Sidonians: the inhabitants of Sidon, which lies on the Mediterranean Sea in Lebanon.

3.2.4.en: Mount Baal-hermon: which is now called Mount Hermon (Jebel el-Sheikh), where there was a temple of Baal (Map 12). The entering in of Hamath: a city on the Orontes River in Syria.

3.2.5.en: He mentions here the peoples whom the children of Israel did not drive out, who dwelt with them and troubled them afterward when they mingled with them. Joshua had captured three of the great Philistine cities, which are Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron, and Judah followed him (ch. 1:18), and Shamgar followed him when he fought the Philistines and killed six hundred men of them (ch. 3:31), but the Philistines were afterward able to recover their cities, and enmity and wars continued between the children of Israel and the Philistines.

3.3.0.en: Those are the ones God allowed to be left, in order to show in the following generations how far Israel would obey the Lord, and whether they would be influenced by the immoral ways of pagan worship or keep their faithfulness to the Lord their God.

3.3.1.en: God allows the presence of evil around you, not for you to fall into it, but for you to hold fast to God and seek His help, so that evil has no authority over you, but He removes it from you and lets you enjoy His fellowship.

3.4.0.en: The Hittites: the sons of Heth, son of Canaan.

3.4.1.en: The Amorites: the inhabitants of the mountainous regions.

3.4.2.en: The Perizzites: the inhabitants of the villages.

3.4.3.en: The Hivites: the inhabitants of the northeastern part of Palestine.

3.4.4.en: The Jebusites: the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

3.4.5.en: He mentions here six of the original peoples of the land, groups of whom remained because the children of Israel were negligent in driving them out, so they mingled with them and intermarried with them, against God's repeated commands (Deut 7:23), and they worshiped their idols under the influence of their pagan wives.

3.5.0.en: Baalim: the plural of Baal, who is the sun god.

3.5.1.en: Groves: wooden pillars carved with images of pagan gods.

3.5.2.en: By this the children of Israel forsook God and worshiped the pagan gods, the most important of which were Baal and Ashtaroth, for whom they set up the pillars.

3.6.0.en: Mesopotamia (Aram-naharaim): the land between the Tigris and the Euphrates.

3.6.1.en: Chushan-rishathaim: a name meaning Chushan of the double wickedness.

3.6.2.en: The Lord was greatly angered against His people because of what they did in the previous verses, so He allowed the king of Aram to prevail over them and enslave them for eight years.

3.7.0.en: Othniel: a name meaning the power of God.

3.7.1.en: Because of the humiliation of slavery the people cried out to God and repented, so He had compassion on them and sent them a judge, Othniel, the younger brother of Caleb, who fought the city of Kirjath-sepher and possessed it and married Achsah, the daughter of Caleb (Josh 15:17). Othniel led them and defeated the Arameans and delivered his people. It should be noted that the strength and wisdom that were in Othniel were the result of the Holy Spirit coming upon him, so his hand prevailed, that is, grew strong, against Chushan and he defeated him.

3.8.0.en: After their victory over the Arameans and their deliverance from their slavery, the people of God lived in rest for 40 years, that is, they lived without slavery and without mingling with idols and evil desires. And after 40 years Othniel died.

3.8.1.en: The Spirit of God dwelling in you is able to give you strength and wisdom in every circumstance of life, so that you dwell in peace and overcome the evils you meet, if you submit to the Holy Spirit by keeping God's commandments and by repentance.

3.9.0.en: Eglon: a name meaning a fat calf.

3.9.1.en: Moab: a son of Lot; they are peoples who live east of the Dead Sea.

3.9.2.en: After the death of Othniel, the people turned away from the worship of God and worshiped idols when they mingled with the pagan peoples. Because of their negligence and their departure from God, He allowed the king of Moab to rise against them and enslave them. This shows the importance of the servant and his leading of others, and on the other hand the importance of steadfastness in the spiritual life and holding fast to the worship of God.

3.10.0.en: The Ammonites: the sons of Ammon, son of Lot, who lived east of the Jordan, to the north of Moab.

3.10.1.en: The Amalekites: tribes that lived in Sinai and whom Moses defeated under the leadership of Joshua (Ex 17). Eglon allied himself with two other peoples, the sons of Ammon and Amalek, and attacked the children of Israel and defeated them and killed many of them, then took the city of palm trees, that is, Jericho. Most likely Eglon attacked them by crossing the Jordan River at a time when its waters were low, and he fought them and took possession of their land and enslaved them for eighteen years. We note here that the period of slavery increased, because Chushan-rishathaim, king of Aram, had enslaved them for eight years (v. 8), and God allowed the affliction upon them to increase until they should repent, because they were negligent the first time after God had given them rest, and returned to the worship of idols and various desires.

3.11.0.en: The people suffered the humiliation of slavery and were pricked in their hearts, so they cried out to the Lord, and the Lord in His wide mercy never overlooks the cry of the distressed and accepts their return to Him. So He appointed a deliverer for them, Ehud the son of Gera, of the tribe of Benjamin, who was left-handed, that is, he used his left hand (ambidextrous). The people sent with him a valuable present for Eglon, king of Moab; it was large in size, so a number of men carried it with him, and its apparent purpose was to appease Eglon so that he would lighten his enslavement of the children of Israel, while the hidden purpose will appear in the following verses.

3.12.0.en: Ehud made for himself a sword sharp on both sides, about half a meter long, that is, relatively short, so that he could hide it under his clothes when he went in to King Eglon, and he girded it on his right thigh, for he was left-handed, since the sword is usually placed on the left thigh by one who uses his right hand. This also helped him to hide it from the eyes of those watching at the king's door.

3.13.0.en: Ehud presented the present to King Eglon, who was very pleased with it, which made him feel safe with Ehud who presented it and not expect any evil from him, as we shall see in what follows. Eglon was a very fat man.

3.14.0.en: With Ehud were several men who had accompanied him to carry the present. After presenting it to the king, Ehud sent them away so that he would be alone when he returned to the king, as will come in the rest of the story, so that no one would be suspicious of the number of men accompanying him.

3.15.0.en: The carved images that were at Gilgal: these are carved statues of the gods and idols, and pillars for the gods.

3.15.1.en: Keep silence: an imperative verb meaning be quiet, that is, he silenced his guards and sent them away from him.

3.15.2.en: Ehud sent away his companions who carried the present, and he returned alone from the statues of the gods and the carved idols in the region of the city of Gilgal to where the king and his attendants were, and he spoke to the king saying that he had a very secret matter that he wished to tell him. So the king commanded everyone to keep silence, and this command of his was a sign meaning that the men should leave from around him to make room for the bearer of the message to speak to the king in secret. This shows the grace God gave Ehud in the eyes of Eglon, so that he trusted him and sent his guards away from him.

3.16.0.en: A summer parlor: a room on an upper floor with a pleasant atmosphere in summer. The king sat in it away from the heat of the weather, since the air enters it from more than one side. It was for the king alone.

3.16.1.en: Ehud went in to the king while he was sitting in the summer parlor, and to give importance to his words, Ehud claimed that the message was directed from God to the king. So the king rose out of respect and reverence for God, for the pagan kings and peoples had a religious sense despite their ignorance of the true God. This confirms Ehud's courage and faith in God in his speech, and then Eglon's submission and his trust in Ehud's words because this was from God.

3.17.0.en: Quickly and skillfully Ehud drew the sword from under his clothes with his left hand and struck the king with it in the belly.

3.18.0.en: The haft: the handle of the sword.

3.18.1.en: The blade: the weapon part of the sword.

3.18.3.en: The haft went in after the blade, the whole blade, into the king's belly, for he struck him hard, and since the king was very fat the blade disappeared in the king's belly, for the fat of his fleshy body covered it, and Ehud did not draw the sword out but left it in his belly. The sword went through in its full length in his belly and its pointed end came out below the king's body, that is, from between the thighs at the anus, and this is an interpretation of the word "dirt". There is another opinion, which may be the more likely, that the pronoun in the verb "came out" refers to Ehud and not the sword, and that the word translated "dirt" means the window, which looked out on a porch or corridor leading to the porch, so Ehud went out through it after shutting the doors of the parlor from the inside firmly, that is, with the key, and passed through the porch and met the guards and greeted them and then departed. This shows the extent of Ehud's faith and steadfastness.

3.19.0.en: Covereth his feet: a polite expression meaning that the king is relieving himself in the toilet.

3.19.1.en: When Ehud left, the king's men came and saw the doors locked, and they thought that the king was in the bathroom relieving himself, and for that reason had locked the doors of the parlor, and that they must wait outside. The meaning of "covereth his feet" may be that he was asleep with his feet covered with a sheet or some other cover, so they were ashamed to open the doors lest they wake him from his sleep.

3.20.0.en: They stayed a long time without the king opening the doors for them as they were expecting him to do after he relieved himself or got up from his sleep. They fell into perplexity and embarrassment, but finally decided to open the door of the parlor, and as soon as they entered they were horrified to find the king lying on the ground dead.

3.21.0.en: The king's men remained amazed and overwhelmed by the horror of the situation, almost lost in their thoughts, not knowing how to act. This confusion of theirs helped Ehud to make use of the time to flee and save himself, so he passed the carved stones at Gilgal and continued his way until he reached Seirath, a place full of trees in the mountains of Ephraim, and hid there, and so he was safe.

3.22.0.en: When Ehud came to Seirath he blew the trumpet so that the people would gather to him. The people heard the sound of the trumpet and answered the call, and he went down from the mountain, that is, from Seirath which lies in the mountain of Ephraim, and the people followed him to fight the Moabites.

3.23.0.en: The fords of Jordan: the Jordan River at the time of its low water, for people could wade through it on foot at certain places, whose number was about fifty.

3.23.1.en: Ehud asked the people to follow him to face the Moabites because he realized that the death of the king would be followed by the collapse of the whole people. The Jordan River had many fords at the time of its low water, so that they could be crossed on foot, so Ehud and his men took control of the fords, and by this they separated the Moabite forces stationed west of the Jordan from the rest of their armies that were east of the Jordan, so that the one could not help the other.

3.24.0.en: The Moabite forces west of the Jordan became almost besieged, so the children of Israel overpowered them and killed about ten thousand warriors of them, every one who was able to fight and every mighty man, that is, they were all killed and not one escaped.

3.25.0.en: Moab was subdued under the hand of Israel: the Moabites were defeated before Israel and submitted to them, and the Israelites gained dominion over them.

3.25.1.en: With the destruction of the king of the Moabites and his army, they submitted to the rule of the children of Israel, and humiliation and disgrace came upon them. By this deliverance that Ehud achieved, peace, quiet and security returned to the land of Israel, and the land had rest from the harshness of subjection to the pagan peoples for eighty years.

3.25.2.en: Ehud risked his life to rescue his people, and God saved him. Let us labor in the service of our brethren and not be afraid, for God will keep us and uphold us and bless our service.

3.26.0.en: An ox goad: a long stick that was used to prick any animal if it lagged in its walking.

3.26.1.en: The Philistines were among the fiercest enemies of Israel, and they were always hostile to them, contending with them over the possession of lands in the regions near the coast of the Mediterranean Sea. A war arose between them during which Israel was led by one of the judges whom the Lord raised up, "Shamgar the son of Anath", who was a contemporary of Ehud, and Shamgar used a pointed piece of iron suitable as a goad for pricking oxen, and with it he killed six hundred men of the Philistine army. That was enough to discipline the Philistines, so they ceased troubling the children of Israel. Here appears Shamgar's faith in the power of God that supported him against the enemies, for although he had no weapons available, he used the ox goad, a weak instrument, to fight with it the armies of the enemies that numbered in the thousands, and killed six hundred men of them, and the rest were afraid and fled. He did not rely on human strength, but God gave him courage, since he believed in Him, to attack the enemies alone so that they feared him, and he gave peace to his people.

3.26.2.en: God uses the weakest of persons and the simplest of tools to carry out His plan and fulfill His good will. Here He delivers His people by an ox goad, just as He helped Samson, who killed a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass, and David faced Goliath with a sling and a stone, and He even used simple apostles to spread the Gospel in the whole world. God works through all for the glory of His name and the salvation of those who love Him. So do not fear your weakness, but come forward with confidence to serve God and live with Him.
